hello.title: Hello, Ruby
hello.summary: Write your first Ruby programs: print text and numbers with puts, print and p, and let Ruby calculate.
hello.lesson.0: Ruby is a programming language that is easy to read. A Ruby program is a list of instructions. The computer runs them from top to bottom, one line after the other. Your first instruction is `puts`: it prints a value and then starts a new line.
hello.lesson.2: Text in quotes is called a **string**. You can write it with double quotes, `"Hi"`, or with single quotes, `'Hi'`. Every `puts` prints its own line.
hello.lesson.5: Numbers need no quotes. Ruby calculates with `+` (plus), `-` (minus), `*` (times) and `/` (divided by). Whole numbers are called **integers**. When you divide two integers, Ruby drops the part after the decimal point: `7 / 2` is `3`. Write `7.0 / 2` to get `3.5`. `%` gives the remainder of a division: `7 % 2` is `1`.
hello.lesson.7: Quotes make a big difference. `"2"` with quotes is text, `2` without quotes is a number. `+` between two strings joins them, and `+` between two numbers adds them.
hello.lesson.10: `print` prints a value **without** a new line at the end, so the next output continues on the same line. `p` prints a value the way Ruby sees it: a string keeps its quotes. Programmers use `p` to check values while they work.
hello.lesson.12: Everything after a `#` on a line is a **comment**. Ruby ignores it. In this course, comments only show results, for example `puts 2 + 3 # 5`.
hello.card.0: `puts "Hi"` prints and starts a new line
hello.card.2: `p "Hi"` shows the value as Ruby sees it: `"Hi"`
hello-1.prompt: Which line prints Hello and then starts a new line?
hello-1.explain: `puts` prints the value and starts a new line. `print` does not start a new line, `echo` does not exist in Ruby, and `Hello` without quotes is not a string.
hello-3.explain: Both numbers are integers, so Ruby drops the part after the decimal point: 9 / 2 is 4, not 4.5.
hello-4.explain: `print` does not start a new line and adds no space, so both strings end up next to each other.
hello-5.explain: `"2"` and `"3"` are strings because of the quotes. `+` joins two strings, so the result is `23`.
hello-6.prompt: Complete the code so it prints 3.5.
hello-6.explain: With `7.0`, one number is a float, so the result keeps the decimal part: `3.5`. `7 / 2` gives `3`, and you cannot divide a string.
hello-7.prompt: Match each piece of code with what it does.
hello-7.pairs.0: prints and starts a new line
hello-7.pairs.2: shows the value as Ruby sees it
hello-8.prompt: Build a line that prints the result of 10 minus 4 and starts a new line.
hello-8.explain: `puts` prints the result, `6`, and starts a new line. The numbers need no quotes.
hello-9.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints: Hello, Ruby!
hello-9.explain: `print` keeps everything on one line. The last line uses `puts`, so the output ends with a new line.
hello-10.prompt: This program should print Start, 12 and End on three lines. Which line has the bug?
hello-10.explain: Ruby multiplies with `*`, not with `x`. Write `puts 3 * 4`.
hello-11.explain: `p` shows the value the way Ruby sees it, so a string keeps its double quotes.
hello-12.prompt: This program should print: Hi, Sam! Which line has the bug?
hello-12.explain: Text needs quotes. Without them, Ruby looks for something called `Sam` and stops with an error. Write `print "Sam"`.
variables.title: Variables and types
variables.summary: Store values in variables, meet Integer, Float, String, true, false and nil, and put values into text with #{}.
variables.lesson.0: A **variable** is a name for a value. You create it with `=`: the name on the left, the value on the right. After that, you use the name instead of the value.
variables.lesson.2: A variable can get a new value later; Ruby then forgets the old one. `score += 5` is short for `score = score + 5`, and `score -= 1` is short for `score = score - 1`. Variable names use small letters and underscores, like `first_name`.
variables.lesson.5: Every value has a type, which Ruby calls its **class**. `.class` asks a value for its class. Whole numbers are `Integer`, numbers with a decimal point are `Float`, and text is `String`. `true` and `false` answer yes-or-no questions. `nil` means "no value".
variables.lesson.7: `puts nil` prints an empty line, because `nil` has no text. `p nil` shows `nil`.
variables.lesson.9: To put a value into a string, write `#{}` inside **double quotes** and put a variable or a calculation between the braces. This is called **interpolation**. It does not work with single quotes.
variables.lesson.11: You cannot join a string and a number with `+`: `"Age: " + 12` stops with an error (`TypeError`). Convert the value first. `.to_s` turns a value into a string, `.to_i` turns a string into an integer, and `.to_f` turns it into a float.
variables.card.2: `"Hi #{name}"` puts a value into a string (double quotes only)
variables-1.explain: `x` starts as `5`. The second line stores `5 * 2`, so `x` is `10`.
variables-2.explain: `7.5` has a decimal point, so its class is `Float`.
variables-3.explain: Inside double quotes, `#{name}` is replaced with the value of `name`.
variables-4.explain: Interpolation only works in double quotes. In single quotes, `#{name}` stays as it is, so the program prints `Hello, #{name}`.
variables-5.prompt: Complete the code so it prints: Total: 15
variables-5.explain: `+` can only join a string with another string. `.to_s` turns the number `15` into the string `"15"`.
variables-6.prompt: Match each value with its type.
variables-6.pairs.1: a number with a decimal point (Float)
variables-7.prompt: Build a line that stores the sum of a and b in the variable total.
variables-7.explain: The name of the new variable comes first, then `=`, then the value to store.
variables-8.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints 8.
variables-8.explain: `count` must exist before you use it. 3 times 2 is 6, plus 2 is 8. In the other order, you would get (3 + 2) * 2 = 10.
variables-9.prompt: This program should print: Score: 10. Which line has the bug?
variables-9.explain: You cannot join a string and an integer with `+`. Write `text = "Score: " + score.to_s`, or use interpolation: `"Score: #{score}"`.
variables-10.explain: `"3".to_i` turns the string into the integer `3`, and `3 + 4` is `7`.
variables-11.explain: `b = a` stores the value that `a` has at that moment, `10`. Changing `a` later does not change `b`.
variables-12.prompt: This program should print: Hi, Max! Which line has the bug?
strings.title: Strings
strings.summary: Change and check text with string methods like upcase, length, include? and gsub, and take parts of a string.
strings.lesson.0: A **method** is an action that a value can do. You call it with a dot after the value, like `"hello".upcase`. `upcase` gives the text in capital letters, `downcase` in small letters, and `capitalize` makes only the first letter a capital.
strings.lesson.2: `length` counts the characters of a string; spaces count too. `reverse` gives the characters in reverse order.
strings.lesson.4: Some methods need extra information. You pass it in parentheses `()`; it is called an **argument**. A method name that ends with `?` answers a question with `true` or `false`. `include?` checks if a string contains some text, `start_with?` and `end_with?` check the beginning and the end, and `empty?` checks if a string has no characters.
strings.lesson.7: `gsub(a, b)` replaces **every** `a` with `b`. `sub(a, b)` replaces only the first one. `strip` removes spaces at the start and the end. You can call one method after the other: `"  hi  ".strip.upcase` first removes the spaces, then makes capitals.
strings.lesson.9: These methods return a **new** string; the original stays the same. Store the result if you need it: `word = word.upcase`.
strings.lesson.12: Each character has a position, called its **index**. The first index is `0`, not `1`. `word[0]` is the first character and `word[-1]` is the last one. `word[start, count]` takes `count` characters, beginning at index `start`.
strings.card.4: `s[0]` is the first character, `s[-1]` the last, `s[1, 3]` three from index 1
strings-1.explain: `banana` has six characters: b, a, n, a, n, a.
strings-2.explain: Indexes start at `0`: `word[0]` is `R`, so `word[1]` is `u`.
strings-3.explain: `[1, 3]` starts at index `1` (`e`) and takes three characters: `ell`.
strings-5.explain: `upcase` returns a new string, but the program does not store it. `text` is still `hello`.
strings-6.prompt: Complete the code so it prints true.
strings-6.explain: The method is called `include?`, with a question mark, because it answers a yes-or-no question.
strings-7.prompt: Match each piece of code with what it gives.
strings-8.prompt: Build a line that replaces every a with o and stores the result in text.
strings-8.explain: `gsub` replaces every `a`, and `text =` stores the new string. `sub` would replace only the first `a`.
strings-9.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints YBUR.
strings-9.explain: Each line uses the variable that the line before it creates: `ruby`, then `RUBY`, then `YBUR`.
strings-10.prompt: This program should print the first letter, R. Which line has the bug?
strings-10.explain: The first index is `0`, so `word[1]` is `u`. Write `first = word[0]`.
strings-11.explain: `capitalize` makes the first letter of the string a capital and all other letters small.
strings-12.prompt: This program should print 4. Which line has the bug?
strings-12.explain: The method name is misspelled, so Ruby does not know it. Write `count = name.length`.
conditions.title: Decisions
conditions.summary: Let your program choose with if, elsif, else and unless, compare values, combine conditions and use case and when.
conditions.lesson.0: A comparison gives `true` or `false`. `==` checks if two values are equal; remember that one `=` stores a value and two compare. `!=` means "not equal". `<`, `>`, `<=` and `>=` mean less than, greater than, less or equal, and greater or equal.
conditions.lesson.2: `if` runs code only when its condition is `true`. The code after `else` runs when it is `false`. `end` closes the whole block. Indent the code inside by two spaces: Ruby does not need it, but it makes the code easy to read.
conditions.lesson.4: `elsif` checks another condition when the ones before it were `false`. Ruby tests the conditions from top to bottom and runs only the first branch that matches.
conditions.lesson.6: `&&` means **and**: both sides must be `true`. `||` means **or**: one true side is enough. `!` turns `true` into `false` and `false` into `true`. `unless` is the opposite of `if`: its code runs when the condition is `false`.
conditions.lesson.8: For one short line, you can put `if` or `unless` at the end: `puts "Hot" if temperature > 30`. The **ternary operator** `condition ? a : b` gives `a` when the condition is `true` and `b` when it is `false`.
conditions.lesson.11: `case` compares one value with several options. Each `when` lists one or more values, separated by commas. The code after `else` runs when no `when` matches.
conditions.lesson.13: In Ruby, only `false` and `nil` count as false in a condition. Every other value counts as true, even `0` and the empty string `""`.
conditions-2.explain: `85 >= 90` is `false`, `85 >= 80` is `true`. Ruby runs only the first matching branch, so it prints `B` and skips the rest.
conditions-3.explain: Only `false` and `nil` count as false in Ruby. `0` counts as true, so the `if` branch runs.
conditions-4.explain: `a > 3` is `true`, but `b < 5` is `false`. With `&&`, both sides must be `true`.
conditions-5.prompt: Complete the code so it prints Different.
conditions-5.explain: `!=` means "not equal". `4 != 5` is `true`. Ruby has no `<>` operator.
conditions-6.prompt: Match each piece of code with its meaning.
conditions-6.pairs.3: runs when the condition is false
conditions-7.prompt: Build a line that prints Hot only when temp is greater than 30.
conditions-7.explain: A short `if` can come at the end of the line: first the action, then `if` and the condition.
conditions-8.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints Cold.
conditions-8.explain: The variable comes first. `10 > 20` is `false`, so the `else` branch prints `Cold`. `end` closes the `if`.
conditions-9.prompt: This program should print Wrong. Which line has the bug?
conditions-9.explain: One `=` stores `7` in `answer`, and `7` counts as true. To compare, use two: `if answer == 7`.
conditions-10.explain: `x` is `nil`, and `nil` counts as false. So the ternary operator gives the second value, `no`.
conditions-11.explain: `Mon` matches no `when`, so the `else` branch runs.
conditions-12.prompt: This program should print positive. Which line has the bug?
conditions-12.explain: Ruby spells it `elsif`, without the second e. Ruby reads `elseif` as an unknown method and stops with an error. Write `elsif n < 0`.
loops.title: Loops and ranges
loops.summary: Repeat code with times, each, upto and while, and count through ranges like 1..5.
loops.lesson.0: A **loop** repeats code. The easiest loop in Ruby is `times`: `3.times` runs the code three times. The code between `do` and `end` is called a **block**.
loops.lesson.2: A block can receive a value between two bars, like `|i|`. With `times`, `i` counts from `0`. For short blocks, you can use curly braces `{ }` instead of `do` and `end`.
loops.lesson.5: A **range** is a sequence of values from a start to an end. `1..5` contains 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5. With three dots, `1...5` stops **before** the end: 1, 2, 3 and 4. `each` runs a block once for every value. Ranges also have methods: `sum` adds all values, and `include?` checks if a value is part of the range.
loops.lesson.7: `upto` counts up from one number to another, and `downto` counts down.
loops.lesson.10: A `while` loop repeats its code as long as its condition is `true`. Make sure that the code in the loop changes the condition; otherwise, the loop never stops.
loops.lesson.12: `break` leaves a loop at once. `next` skips the rest of the block and continues with the next value. `n.even?` is `true` for even numbers, and `n.odd?` for odd numbers.
loops.card.2: `(1..5).each do |n| … end` runs once for every value
loops-1.explain: The block runs four times, and `print` adds no new line, so you get four stars on one line.
loops-2.explain: `1...4` stops before 4, so the loop adds 1 + 2 + 3 = 6.
loops-3.explain: The block runs five times and adds 2 each time: 5 times 2 is 10.
loops-4.explain: `1..5` includes 5. `1...5`, with three dots, stops before 5.
loops-5.prompt: Complete the code so it prints the numbers 1, 2 and 3 on three lines.
loops-5.explain: `1.upto(3)` counts up from 1 to 3. `downto` counts down, and `times` does not take an argument.
loops-6.prompt: Match each piece of code with its meaning.
loops-7.prompt: Build a line that prints every number from 1 to 5.
loops-7.explain: Two dots include the 5. The block receives each number as `n` between bars and prints it.
loops-8.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints 3, 2 and 1 on three lines.
loops-8.explain: `n` must exist before the loop. Inside the loop, the program prints `n` first and then makes it smaller; in the other order, it would print 2, 1 and 0.
loops-9.prompt: This program should print the numbers 1 to 5. Which line has the bug?
loops-9.explain: Three dots stop before 5, so the program prints only 1 to 4. Write `(1..5).each do |n|`.
loops-10.explain: When `n` is 4, `break` leaves the loop before `print` runs. So only 1, 2 and 3 are printed.
loops-11.explain: `next` skips the odd numbers, so only 2, 4 and 6 are printed, on one line.
loops-12.prompt: This program should count down 5, 4, 3, 2, 1 and then print Go! Which line has the bug?
loops-12.explain: `upto` counts up, so `5.upto(1)` runs zero times. Write `5.downto(1) do |i|`.
methods.title: Methods
methods.summary: Write your own methods with def, give them parameters and default values, and return results.
methods.lesson.0: A **method** is a named piece of code that you can run again and again. You define it with `def`, a name, the code, and `end`. You **call** the method by writing its name.
methods.lesson.2: **Parameters** are variables in parentheses after the method name. When you call the method, you give it values for them; these values are the **arguments**. Separate several parameters with commas.
methods.lesson.4: A parameter can have a **default value**: `def greet(name = "friend")`. When you call the method without an argument, Ruby uses the default.
methods.lesson.7: A method gives back a value, its **return value**: the value of the last line that runs. You do not need to write `return` for it. Use `return` to leave a method early with a value.
methods.lesson.9: Methods that answer a yes-or-no question end with `?` and return `true` or `false`, like `even?`. You can name your own methods the same way.
methods.lesson.11: A method that ends with `!` usually changes the value itself instead of returning a new one. `upcase` returns a new string; `upcase!` changes the string that is stored in the variable.
methods.lesson.13: A variable that you create outside a method does not exist inside it, and the other way round. Give values to a method as arguments, and get results back as the return value.
methods.card.3: The last line gives the return value; `return` leaves early
methods.card.4: `?` methods answer yes or no; `!` methods change the value
methods-1.explain: The last line of the method, `n * 2`, is its return value: 21 times 2 is 42.
methods-2.explain: The call has no argument, so `name` gets its default value, `"you"`.
methods-3.explain: The arguments go to the parameters in order: `width` is 3, `height` is 4, and 3 times 4 is 12.
methods-4.statement: A method can use a variable that you created outside of it.
methods-4.explain: A method has its own variables. A variable from outside does not exist inside the method; pass the value as an argument instead.
methods-5.prompt: Complete the code so it prints 9.
methods-5.explain: Every `def` needs an `end` that closes the method.
methods-6.prompt: Match each piece of code with its meaning.
methods-6.pairs.1: leaves the method with a value
methods-6.pairs.2: a method that answers yes or no
methods-7.prompt: Build a line that leaves the method early with "negative" when n is less than 0.
methods-7.explain: `return` gives back the value and leaves the method at once. The `if` at the end makes it happen only when `n < 0`.
methods-8.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints 15.
methods-8.explain: You define the method first, with `def` and `end` around its code. Then you can call it.
methods-9.prompt: This program should print 10. Which line has the bug?
methods-9.explain: The method uses `b` and gets two arguments, but it has only one parameter. Write `def add(a, b)`.
methods-10.explain: `3 < 10` is `true`, so `return` leaves the method with `"small"`. The last line does not run.
methods-11.explain: `capitalize!` with `!` changes the string in `name` itself.
methods-12.prompt: This program should print true, because 4 is even. Which line has the bug?
methods-12.explain: An even number has the remainder `0` when you divide it by 2. Write `n % 2 == 0`.
collections.title: Arrays and hashes
collections.summary: Keep many values in arrays and hashes, use symbols as keys, and work with each, map, select and sum.
collections.lesson.0: An **array** is an ordered list of values in square brackets `[]`, separated by commas. Each element has an index, starting at `0`, like the characters of a string. `p` shows the whole array.
collections.lesson.2: `<<` adds an element at the end. `first` and `last` give the first and the last element, `include?` checks if a value is in the array, and `sort` returns a sorted copy.
collections.lesson.4: `each` runs a block for every element. `map` builds a new array from the results of the block. `select` keeps only the elements for which the block gives `true`. `sum`, `min` and `max` work on arrays of numbers.
collections.lesson.6: `join` turns an array into one string. Its argument goes between the elements: `["a", "b", "c"].join(", ")` gives `a, b, c`.
collections.lesson.8: A **hash** stores pairs of a **key** and a **value** in curly braces `{}`. You get a value with its key in square brackets. Keys are often **symbols**: names with a colon in front, like `:name`. A symbol is a fixed label. In a hash, `name: "Ana"` is short for the key `:name` with the value `"Ana"`.
collections.lesson.10: Keys can also be strings; then you write `=>` between the key and the value. A key that is not in the hash gives `nil`. `each` on a hash gives the block two values: the key and the value.
collections.lesson.12: `:name` and `"name"` are different keys. If you store a value with the symbol `:name`, you must also read it with `:name`.
collections.card.3: `:name` is a symbol; a missing key gives `nil`
collections-1.explain: Indexes start at `0`: `nums[0]` is 4, so `nums[1]` is 7.
collections-2.explain: `map` builds a new array with the result of the block for every element: each number plus 1.
collections-4.explain: `person[:age]` gives the value stored under the key `:age`.
collections-5.explain: The hash has no key `"Ben"`, so `ages["Ben"]` gives `nil`, and `p` shows it as `nil`.
collections-6.prompt: Complete the code so it prints [2, 4].
collections-6.explain: `select` keeps the elements for which the block gives `true`. `map` would give `[false, true, false, true]`.
collections-7.prompt: Match each piece of code with its meaning.
collections-8.prompt: Build a line that prints all numbers in nums doubled.
collections-8.explain: `map` builds a new array from the results of the block, and `p` shows it.
collections-9.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints Ana: 30 and then Ben: 25.
collections-9.explain: First create the hash. Then `each` gives the block every key and value, in the order you stored them.
collections-10.prompt: This program should print: Hello, Ana! Which line has the bug?
collections-10.explain: The key is the symbol `:name`, not the string `"name"`, so `person["name"]` gives `nil`. Write `name = person[:name]`.
collections-11.explain: `select` keeps the words with more than two characters, `hello` and `hey`. That array has 2 elements.
collections-12.prompt: This program should print the total price, 9. Which line has the bug?
collections-12.explain: `total = price` replaces the total each time, so it ends as 4. Write `total += price` to add every price.
classes.title: Classes
classes.summary: Build your own kinds of objects with class, initialize and instance variables, and add methods, attr_accessor and to_s.
classes.lesson.0: Everything in Ruby is an **object**, and every object belongs to a **class**: `"hi"` is an object of the class `String`. A class is like a blueprint. You define your own class with `class`, a name that starts with a capital letter, and `end`. `new` creates an object of the class.
classes.lesson.2: `initialize` is a special method: `new` calls it when it creates an object, and passes on its arguments. A variable that starts with `@` is an **instance variable**. Each object has its own copy, and all methods of the object can use it.
classes.lesson.5: Code outside the class cannot read instance variables: `rex.name` does not work yet. `attr_reader :name` adds a method `name` that returns `@name`. `attr_accessor :age` adds a method to read `@age` and one to change it with `=`.
classes.lesson.7: Methods can change instance variables. This way, every object keeps its own **state**.
classes.lesson.10: `puts` calls the method `to_s` to turn an object into text, and interpolation with `#{}` does the same. Define `to_s` in your class to decide what your objects look like as text.
classes.lesson.12: Without your own `to_s`, `puts` prints something like `#<Point:0x000…>`: the class name and a memory address.
classes.card.2: `@name` is an instance variable: each object has its own
classes-1.explain: `new` passes `"Tom"` to `initialize`, which stores it in `@name`. `greet` uses `@name`.
classes-2.prompt: Which method does `new` call when it creates an object?
classes-2.explain: `new` creates the object and then calls its `initialize` method with the arguments.
classes-3.explain: `@count` starts at 10. The two calls add 5 and 1, so it ends at 16.
classes-4.explain: The class has no method `name`, so the call stops with an error (`NoMethodError`). Add `attr_reader :name` to the class to fix it.
classes-5.prompt: Complete the code so it prints: Ruby Basics
classes-5.explain: The program reads `title` and also changes it with `b.title =`. Only `attr_accessor` adds both methods.
classes-6.prompt: Match each piece of code with its meaning.
classes-6.pairs.0: defines a new kind of object
classes-6.pairs.1: runs when an object is created
classes-7.prompt: Build a line that creates a Dog named Rex and stores it in pet.
classes-7.explain: `Dog.new` creates the object; the argument `"Rex"` goes to `initialize`.
classes-8.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program defines a class and prints Hi.
classes-8.explain: The method `hello` lives inside the class. Each `end` closes the last open `def` or `class`. After the class, you can create an object and call its method.
classes-9.prompt: This program should print Ana. Which line has the bug?
classes-9.explain: `name = name` only sets the parameter again; `@name` stays `nil`. Write `@name = name`.
classes-10.explain: Interpolation calls `to_s` on the object, and this class defines its own `to_s`.
classes-11.explain: `@on` starts as `false`. Each `switch` flips it: true, false, true.
classes-12.prompt: This program should print: Rex: Woof. Which line has the bug?
classes-12.explain: `initialize` needs a name, so `Dog.new` without an argument stops with an error. Write `rex = Dog.new("Rex")`.
